Why does a tower that is mostly
empty space not crush itself?
Burj Khalifa in Dubai rises 828
meters, higher than any other
building ever finished.
Yet most of it is air:
lobbies, corridors, apartments
and elevator shafts.
A needle that tall and that hollow
should fold under its own weight,
and the wind should finish the job.
So what is really holding it up?
The answer begins with something
you can crush in one hand.
Take a flat sheet of paper.
Stand that sheet on its edge and
it flops over at once.
Now roll the same sheet into a tube.
Suddenly it can carry a surprising load.
The paper did not change.
Only its shape did.
Nature found this trick long ago.
A bird's bones are hollow,
braced by thin struts inside,
which keeps them light and stiff.
Bamboo is a hollow stalk,
stiffened by solid rings along its length.
Hollow shapes put material exactly
where it matters most.
Every skyscraper fights a quiet
war against two invisible enemies.
The first is gravity.
It wants to pull the whole tower
straight down, and the weight is enormous.
Burj Khalifa is often quoted at
roughly half a million tonnes,
even with nobody inside.
The second enemy pushes sideways.
Engineers call it a lateral load,
and for a tower this tall the
biggest one is wind.
In some parts of the world,
earthquakes add another.
Burj Khalifa's chief structural
engineer, Bill Baker of the firm
SOM, has described wind as the
most important factor in designing
tall buildings.
So the puzzle is this.
How do you defeat gravity and wind
using mostly empty air?
We will solve it from the bottom
up, starting far below the streets of Dubai.
Before anything could rise,
engineers had to learn what the
ground could carry.
They drilled test holes across
the site and examined the rock below.
The news was not ideal.
Instead of hard granite,
they found layers of weak to very
weak sandstone and siltstone.
There was another problem hiding
in the groundwater.
It carries salts that attack steel
and concrete over time.
So the foundation was designed
with cathodic protection, a system
meant to slow the corrosion of
buried metal for decades.
Weak rock sounds like a disaster
for the tallest building on Earth.
But the answer was not to find better rock.
The answer was to spread the load.
Engineers drilled close to two
hundred concrete piles, each about
one and a half meters wide,
deep into the ground.
Think of each pile as a long concrete root.
No single pile has to hold the whole tower.
Together, the piles share the weight
among them.
On top of the piles,
engineers built a thick concrete
mat, called a raft foundation.
To see why, picture walking across deep snow.
In high heels, you sink at once,
because your whole weight is focused
on two tiny points.
A snowshoe spreads that same weight
across a broad surface,
and you can walk across the powder.
The raft is an architectural snowshoe.
It ties the piles and the tower
together so they work as one.
The numbers are enormous.
The raft is about 3.7 meters thick,
roughly twelve feet.
The foundation took more than 45,000
cubic meters of concrete,
weighing over 110,000 tonnes.
All of it exists only to spread
out the load of the tower above.
Giant slabs of concrete have a hidden problem.
Curing concrete gives off heat,
and the thicker the slab,
the hotter its middle gets.
In the Dubai desert,
that is even harder to manage.
So engineers tested many concrete
mixes until they found ones that
could handle the heat.
It worked.
When the tower was finished,
it had settled by only about fifty
millimeters, roughly two inches.
Baker called that tiny for a
building of this size.
Now, how do you carry all that
weight up through 828 meters of
mostly empty space?
Engineers call the route the load path.
Every kilogram, from a chair on
a high floor to the marble in
a bathroom, needs an unbroken path
straight down to the foundation.
At the heart of the tower stands
its spine, a hexagonal core of
reinforced concrete running up
through the middle.
In fact, the tower is built of
high-performance concrete from
the foundation all the way up to level 156.
Designers chose concrete for its
mass, stiffness and strength,
and for how well it blocks sound
between floors.
But lifting it was a challenge.
Crews pumped it up through pipes
to the 156th floor,
a vertical pumping record of 606 meters.
Thick, heavy concrete resists every
meter of that climb,
so the mix had to be tested
until it kept flowing under enormous pressure.
Baker described the core as
torsionally stiff, like an axle.
That means it strongly resists twisting.
But a lone spine,
however stiff, is still a tall, thin stick.
In a strong wind it would bend.
It needed help.
The help comes from the tower's famous shape.
Look down on it from above and
you see a letter Y:
a central hexagonal core,
with three wings spreading out around it.
Baker's team called this a buttressed core.
Think of a Gothic cathedral.
Its tall walls would lean outward
if not for the stone buttresses
pressed against them.
Baker used almost exactly that
comparison himself.
The three wings act as stabilizers.
They brace the core,
and they brace one another,
so that they resist the wind together.
Pushing the structure outward also
widens the tower's stance,
and a wide stance is what keeps
something tall from tipping.
A thin vertical stick has become
a stable tripod with a hollow heart.
The tower does not need to be
solid to be strong.
It only needs its material in the
right places.
There is still a puzzle.
When wind pushes against the side
of the tower, the core wants to
bend one way, while the outer parts
of the wings stand independently.
How do you force these separate
pieces to work as one team?
Picture a skier racing down a snowy slope.
With arms tucked in,
a bump knocks them off balance.
But spread the ski poles out and
plant them in the snow,
and the skier gets a wide,
steady base that keeps the body from tumbling.
Tall buildings use the same idea,
called outriggers.
Burj Khalifa reportedly ties its
vertical structure together at
the mechanical floors with outrigger
walls, which are meant to make
the whole building stiffer.
When wind pushes on the tower,
those walls help pass the push
from the core out to the rest
of the structure.
The side facing the wind is pulled
into tension, while the far side
is squeezed into compression.
The building resists the storm
with leverage, not with brute mass.
Gravity is steady.
Wind is not.
As you climb higher,
the air changes.
At street level, trees,
hills and other buildings break
the wind into gentle pieces.
Hundreds of meters up,
almost nothing slows it down,
and it rushes past with enormous force.
When wind meets a flat wall,
it cannot pass through.
It must go around.
As it slides past the corners,
it peels away from the surface
and forms swirls of air called vortices.
They do not form evenly.
A swirl forms on one side,
breaks away, and then another forms
on the opposite side.
This is called vortex shedding.
Each swirl gives the building a
small sideways push, first one
way, then the other,
in a steady rhythm.
Here is the danger.
Every tall building has a natural
rhythm at which it likes to sway.
If the swirls arrive at that same
rhythm, the pushes add up,
just like a child pumping their
legs on a playground swing.
Each push makes the motion bigger.
This is called resonance.
Left unchecked, the swaying grows.
It could stress the structure,
damage the facade and make the
upper floors uncomfortable to live in.
This is the real nightmare for
a skyscraper designer, because
no amount of extra concrete simply fixes it.
So how do you tame this invisible beast?
Not with brute strength.
The designers used wind tunnels.
The studies were run by an
engineering firm called RWDI,
in Guelph, Ontario, in Canada.
They tested small models of the
tower while air blasted past,
and measured the forces on them.
Baker later recalled that the first
tests showed their initial design
would not work.
So they reshaped it,
again and again.
Baker said you do not accept the
wind as a given.
It is part of the design process,
and the team kept reshaping the
building until its shape worked
with the wind instead of against it.
The result is a tower that tapers
as it rises.
Its edges are softened into
scalloped steps, and those steps
spiral up the tower.
A museum exhibit describes the
goal in three words:
confuse the wind.
Here is why that works.
Because the shape changes at every
level, the wind cannot find one
steady rhythm along the whole height.
A swirl forming at one height does
not line up with a swirl forming at another.
Instead of one coordinated push,
the wind breaks into small,
disorganized eddies.
The payoff was huge.
The original design was reportedly
about 518 meters tall.
Refining the shape against the
wind helped the tower grow all
the way to 828 meters,
roughly three hundred meters taller.
The top of the tower shows the same thinking.
Above level 156, concrete gives
way to a lighter steel frame,
topped by a spire built around
a steel pipe of about 350 tonnes.
Roughly the top thirty percent
of the building's height has no
occupied floors at all.
Have you ever felt a faint movement
standing high in a tall building
on a windy day?
That is not a sign of weakness.
A tall tower is not meant to
be perfectly rigid.
It flexes, and spreads the energy
of each gust through its structure.
Burj Khalifa is reported to sway
about one and a half meters at
its very top.
Baker said that it moves much less
than many buildings that are half as tall.
A moving structure brings a new problem.
Whatever covers the frame must
move with it.
More than twenty-six thousand
reflective glass panels clad the tower.
If they were bolted rigidly to
a flexing frame, they would be
pinched and cracked, so tall
buildings use facade systems
designed to follow the motion of the frame.
And how do engineers know a tower
behaves as designed?
They watch it.
Monitoring programs tracked the
foundation's settlement and the
strain in vertical elements such
as walls and columns,
along with the building's movement
and vibration.
A separate full-scale monitoring
program used accelerometers,
anemometers and GPS units on the tower.
Accelerometers feel the shaking,
anemometers measure the wind,
and GPS tracks where the top sits.
The data was logged and delivered
in real time to the operations
and design teams.
Step back and the paradox returns.
How can something mostly made of
air stand fearless against gravity
and the force of the wind?
Because emptiness is not the absence
of strength.
It is the canvas on which geometry,
physics and materials do their quiet work.
Look at what we found.
Piles and a thick raft share the
weight with weak ground.
A concrete spine carries the load.
Three wings brace it like cathedral
buttresses.
Outrigger walls tie the parts together.
A tapering, spiraling shape confuses the wind.
None of it relies on brute mass.
Each part solves one problem,
and together they turn empty space
into a tower that rises above
everything else people have built.
The next time you pass a tall
glass tower, look up and picture
what you cannot see:
roots in the ground,
a spine, buttresses, and a shape
sculpted by the wind.
They are proof that people can
turn emptiness into strength by
working with physics instead of against it.
And the rolled paper tube on your
desk plays by the same rules.
Even when something feels hollow
or empty, the right structure inside
can give it the strength to stand
against the fiercest storms.
